- `github.com/briandowns/...`

So maybe zk uses `github.com/dustin/go-humanize` via a helper. But wait — maybe it's not a helper; maybe the short format template is `{{format-date created "relative"}}` and format-date special-cases the layout "relative"! We saw it printed "relative"... Also — maybe the helper takes 2 args: `{{format-date created "relative" }}` no...

Wait, maybe the relative date comes from `{{format-date created "%r"}}`? No, that's "04:35:27 AM".

Hmm, hold on. What about `{{format-date created}}` where created is a *string*? no.

New angle: maybe the note template's "short" format uses `{{format-date created "%D"}}` = "11/18/26"? no.

Let me test a large brute force. I'll generate candidates from a Python word list? There's no dictionary. Hmm, maybe /usr/share/hunspell? Let me look for any word lists on the system: `find / -name "*words*"` limited.

Alternatively, brute-force 3-letter names (26^3=17576) — at 40ms each = 12 min. Too slow but maybe acceptable? We could speed up by batching multiple candidates in one template! Since unknown functions are silently ignored, and known functions with 1 arg either work or error... Hmm, but if I put many calls in one template and one of them errors (like join), the whole render fails. I can craft calls that take 1 arg and produce no error for known helpers — risky.

Better: use `-f` with a template containing many candidate calls, and check if output is non-empty. If a candidate exists and produces non-empty output, I learn a name. But known helpers might produce empty. Hmm.

distance fuzzytime fuzzy moment timesince timespan when relativetime relative_time ago2 since_now timepast
timeelapsed timediff age datediff format-date format_time shortdate short longdate long humanize-date
humanize_date humandate human-date nice nice-date friendly friendly-date dateago date-ago date_ago relativeago
abs-date abstime rtime timesinceago now-date nowdate""".split()

for b in base: print(b)
PY

text numeric-date""".split()

PY

messages.reasoning_content:
Interesting! Notes created via `touch`:
- `created` is the DB/index time (2026-11-18 04:43:33.27...) — hmm, that's when I ran index. Actually created = index time? Or is created from the note's frontmatter? Hmm, in zk, `created` for a note without frontmatter date is... Let me think. Actually the notes were all created at the same instant (all "just now" with nanosecond differences) — that's the index time. Wait no: created has fractional seconds with increasing values across notes: 33.274, 33.2748, 33.275... They're all at the moment of the *index* run? Hmm, the mtime I set was old, so zk used... 

OH WAIT. Maybe zk stores created = the time when the note was first indexed (i.e., DB insert time), since the note has no creation date in frontmatter. Hmm, but earlier (nb1) the created was 04:35:27.339820892 while modified was 04:35:27.339177665 — both at note-creation time.

Hmm, in nb3 the modified = exact mtime (integer seconds), and created = index time. So for notes without a frontmatter date, zk sets created to... the mtime? In nb3 modified (mtime) is old but created is now. So created is NOT mtime. Hmm! But in nb1, created == modified == note creation time (both from file stat at index time, which was right after creation).

Hmm, in nb3 the mtime was set to old values, but created = index time. So created is derived from the DB insert time? But then in nb1, created would be the index time too — and indeed the index ran right after creation (same second). Yes consistent.

Hmm, but that would be weird. Let me test: touch a file with an old mtime in nb1, re-index with -f (force) and see if created changes... Actually created should not change on re-index (it's stored). Let's test with a NEW notebook: create file, wait 3 seconds, then index, check created. Actually in nb3, index ran after touch, and created = index time. So created = time of first indexing. Hmm, but that contradicts "created" semantics... unless zk uses the frontmatter "Date" field for created, falling back to mtime? Hmm, in nb3 modified = mtime exactly, so zk reads mtime for modified. For created... let me check: is created possibly the *file ctime*? ctime for a touched file = time of the touch. All files were touched at nearly the same moment — but then ctime order would follow the touch order (n0 first? Actually I created files in the loop order n0, n172800, ... wait no, the loop order was n0,5,45,... — and the created values increase in the order n0, n172800, n2592000, ... hmm that doesn't match the loop order (loop order was n0, n5, n45, n59...). Actually the created values are sorted ascending in the listing which is sorted by created! So the order is by created ascending. The listing shows n0, n172800, n2592000, n31536000, ... So creation order (ctime) was n0 first, then n172800, ... hmm that's not the loop order either.

Wait, the default sort order — maybe it's `path`?? No. Let's reconsider: maybe the listing is sorted by created ascending, and created = ctime. Then ctime order = n0, n172800, n2592000, n31536000, n31536001, n3599, ... Hmm, my loop order was: 0,5,45,59,60,61,90,3599,3600,3660,7199,7200,86399,86400,172800,604799,604800,604801,2592000,31536000,31536001. The displayed order: n0, n172800, n2592000, n31536000, n31536001, n3599, n3600, n3660, n45, n5, n59, n60, ... 

Hmm, that looks ALPHABETICAL: n0, n172800, n2592000, n31536000, n31536001, n3599, n3600, n3660, n45, n5, n59, n60, n604799... wait is "n172800" > "n0" alphabetically? "n0" vs "n172800": 'n' then '0' vs '1' → '0' < '1', so n0 first. Then n172800, n2592000? '1' < '2' yes. Then n2592000, n31536000, n31536001, n3599? '3' then '1' < '5' yes. Then n3599, n3600, n3660, n45 ('3' < '4' yes), n5, n59, n60, n604799 ('n5' vs 'n60': '5'<'6' yes), n604800, n604801, n61 ('n604801' vs 'n61': '6'='6','0'<'1' yes), n7199, n7200, n86399, n86400, n90, then... 

So the default sort IS by path/filename ascending! Hmm, but earlier in nb1 the order was lu00.md then ia4f.md — alphabetical would put ia4f.md first! Let me re-check: "ia4f.md" vs "lu00.md" → 'i' < 'l' → ia4f first. But output showed lu00 first. So not alphabetical.

Hmm, so what determines order? In nb3, the created values are all within the same instant but strictly increasing across the listing order. And in nb3's index run, files were processed... in what order? Readdirnames order (filesystem order), which is arbitrary. Then `list` sorted by... hmm, if sorted by created ascending, the order reflects the DB insert order = filesystem order (arbitrary). Alphabetical coincidence? Let's check: is the listing order the alphabetical order? n0,n172800,n2592000,n31536000,n31536001,n3599,n3600,n3660,n45,n5,n59,n60,n604799,n604800,n604801,n61,n7199,n7200,n86399,n86400,n90 — I verified it's alphabetical. That's suspicious: a coincidence would be unlikely for such a weird set. Unless... hmm, files created in loop order and readdir returns... on ext4/overlayfs, directory entries are in hash order, not insertion. 

Hmm, but actually maybe the default sort for `list` is by `path` ascending? Let me verify in nb1 again — lu00.md before ia4f.md contradicts.

Let me test explicitly: in nb3, run `list -s path` and `list -s created` and `list -s created-` and `list -s title` etc, and compare with the default order.

Actually more likely: default sort is `created` DESC? Then n90 (latest) would be first. No.

Hmm. Let me reconsider nb1: notes were lu00.md (created 04:35:27.339820892) and ia4f.md (created 04:37:33.444321286). Order: lu00, ia4f → created ascending. 

In nb3: if created = index time (all ~04:43:33.274...) then order = DB insert order. And the DB insert order = the order zk walked the directory. Hmm, so maybe both are "created ascending".

Let me test nb3's default vs `list -s created` vs `list -s created-` explicitly. And let me check whether created in nb3 = ctime of files. I can test by touching one file again and re-indexing.

Let me investigate created semantics more concretely: create a notebook, create file A, sleep 2, index, sleep 2, create file B, index again, then check created for both. If created for A = index time and B = index time, then created == first index time.

Actually hmm — wait. Maybe created comes from the note's frontmatter `Date` field, and falls back to... hmm, we have no frontmatter.

Hmm, actually maybe zk uses mtime for created when the file is NEW and the DB insert preserves it. In nb3, mtime was old (2020?) no — I used touch -d "now - s", so mtimes were old. If created = mtime, then created would be old. But created is now. So created != mtime.

So created = DB-insert time (index time). Interesting, that's actually a plausible zk behavior? Hmm, in zk I believe created is taken from frontmatter "Date:" else file mtime... Hmm but evidence says otherwise.

Hmm wait, actually maybe zk uses `created = mtime` but I need to double check the mtime I set. `touch -d "@$(( $(date +%s) - s ))"` — sets mtime to past. ctime also changes to now. So created = ctime! ctime for each file = time of the touch (slightly increasing per loop iteration, all within the same second ~04:43:33). That fits: created values 04:43:33.274, .2748, .2750, .2751, .2752, .2754, .2755, .2756, .2757, .2758... These are increasing but each subsequent by ~100-200 microseconds — hmm, that's not consistent with the loop which touches 21 files sequentially (each iteration involves writing a file and touching it; that would take milliseconds, not microseconds). The values span .274 to .277 = 3 milliseconds for 21 files. That's too fast for shell loop (each printf+touch ~ a few ms). Hmm, actually the *listing* is sorted, so the created values in listing order are ascending — and the *values* were assigned by me in the loop over files... 

Hmm no! The listing shows `n0|...04:43:33.274302734` and `n172800|04:43:33.274866643`. The difference is 564 microseconds. In the loop, creating 21 files with printf and touch takes maybe 100ms total → ~5ms per file. So the values should be spread over ~100ms, not 3ms. Unless the order in the listing is alphabetical and the created values just happen to be sorted... but then created values would jump around.

Wait, unless created is assigned per-note at index time (all notes indexed in a single loop within ~3ms!). YES — the index happened in one process run, assigning created = index time per note as it processes each file, incrementing by microseconds. 21 notes in 3ms = 150µs per note — plausible for DB inserts.

Hmm, but then the listing order (alphabetical) is the DB insert order?? The DB insert order would be the filesystem walk order. If zk sorts the walked paths before indexing, then insert order = alphabetical. Hmm! That could be: zk's file walk collects paths sorted.

Actually hmm, wait. Maybe created is NOT the index time but rather... let me test directly. Create a file in nb3, wait 3s, then index and check created. That's decisive.

Let me also test whether list's default sort is `path`.

Let me do these tests.

}
